questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to an English-speaking country to improve my English but also to a place with a great university and lots of history and culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The university is pretty good at taking care of their arriving international students. Most things are compiled on MyEd/Learn (their intranet) for easy access, and if not, the visiting student office are super helpful, and you also get a personal tutor assigned that can assist you with questions.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got most information from emails before my stay and from flyers/information posted on the LEARN site. Also I just emailed the visiting student office or asked someone else - lots of people are in the same boat, so you can almost always find someone who can help you.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was surprisingly easy - but I do think I got really lucky. I found a room in a private flat on
spareroom.co.uk
. I met with my flatmates on Zoom beforehand to view the flat and chat just to see if we were a match. Luckily, they all turned out to be lovely, and the room was cheap. I would really recommend starting to look for rooms/flats at least a few months in advance. The housing market in Edinburgh is very similar to Copenhagen; it is VERY difficult to find anything affordable for a student, and you are not guaranteed university accommodation if you are only staying for one semester.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There are so many amazing parts of the city that you get access to more easily by living off campus. I lived in New Town in Edinburgh, while the campus was in Old Town in the city centre. Although I had a brisk 30 minutes walk to my campus, I did get to spend a lot of time in a part of the city that I normally wouldn't have explored too much.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Student accommodation (through the university) can be insanely expensive. When only studying for one semester, you are not guaranteed a room, and since you get a reply pretty late (shortly before arrival at the university!), it can be really stressful to sort out housing if you rely on getting student accommodation. I'd recommend having a backup plan (e.g. a youth hostel, there are many fairly cheap ones in the city), or at least an idea of the housing market and where to look if you do not get a room.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was fairly easy, although changing courses upon arrival (I realised one course wasn't what I expected it to be) was quite confusing.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You pick the courses you want and prioritise them 1-5 and they give you what they can. I got all of my first 3 priorities but changed one of them later.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The visiting student office and your personal tutor can assist you with courses and course changes.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all of the classes I wanted, even the 4th level course and a high-demand course I didn't expect to get into.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It's fairly straight forward, but be sure to check out the courses outside your field, there are many interesting ones. I didn't take any courses in my own field during my stay abroad.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's strange because the academic level seemed high, but as a visiting student it is difficult to get into anything else than 1st year courses unless it is in the subject you study at home.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: As mentioned above, most subject-specific courses (such as sociology, political science, literature of the ones I wanted to do) require you to have completed 2 years of studies in that subject to have the fundamentals down. This makes it difficult to take courses on your level. I found most of my courses very easy since they were 1st year courses which was both nice since I could focus on other things but also a shame since I wasn't challenged too much academically.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There are almost no teaching hours which I generally don't like. For each course, there was 1 hour lecture, 1 hour tutorial (in class session, usually 5-10 people with a tutor/instructor). The tutorials were the most interesting since you could discuss with your classmates and to practical excersices, but it is not a lot of teaching and a lot of self-study.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introduction to Queer Studies
History of the Scandinavian Novel
Sociology 1B: The sociological imagination: Private troubles, public problems

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I surprisingly found my sociology course very interesting. It taught me different ways to approach a lot of things.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Travelling is insanely expensive in Scotland. We did many day tours out into the country (e.g. we went to Glasgow, Stirling, St. Andrews, Inverness and more), but trains are VERY expensive (I can recommend getting a Railcard from
trainline.co.uk
if you expect to travel a lot by train, it is really worth it), busses as well. I wish I had saved up more money for the longer trips like Isle of Skye, Glencoe etc. where I didn't get to go simply because it was too expensive and very hard when you don't have a car.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Coffee is much cheaper in Edinburgh..... pricing for everything else is more or less the same. Going out, however, is very expensive. They don't have bodegas the same way that we do; a pint costs what a pint costs, the cheapest ones are usually 4 pounds with student discounts. So if you like to go out, be prepared to spend some money.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are societies for almost everything, and it is amazing. During the welcome week, most societies have intro classes, meetings and other free stuff you can attend to see exactly what society fits you. I really do encourage you to go check them out, it is very worth it!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a society! Even if it's a weird one. Try something new. I got into pole dancing while I was away, and it was so much fun and a great way to both exercise and meet new people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel! Go see Scotland. Edinburgh is amazing in itself, but you quickly realise it is very small. Plan ahead for some day trips - there are plenty of places where you can get with coach or train in an hour or two from Edinburgh, and it's a great way to spend your weekend.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. There are so many international people in Edinburgh as well so you can find a bit of everything.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to classes, talk to people you work with, ask them to have a cup of coffee or study together. It's really awkward, yes, but they are most likely not from here as well. Edinburgh has many international students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None that I can think of.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The accents <3

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Plan ahead for your weekends/holidays and take advantage of the fact that you have so much beautiful nature close, don't stress too hard about university (it's in a different language, so everything feels different and harder probably), and please please please don't do like me. Bring a fricking raincoat.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I really do recommend getting housing with likeminded flatmates. My flatmates were all 10-15 years older than me, and although they were lovely, and we had some great times, we didn't have much in common in terms of how we spent our time.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Travelling around Scotland.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Meeting people since Scotland was still in hard lockdown when I arrived.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
